summary: Reconsiders socket-numbering conventions. The Host-Host protocol only said the low-order bit marks socket gender. Two proposals wanted extra network-wide structure, such as a user number for accounting and access control. The authors weigh them and conclude a major NCP overhaul is needed.

eli5.summary: Mailbox numbers only had one rule so far: even for receiving, odd for sending. People wanted more rules, but this note says that would mean big changes.

subtitle: Why two proposals to add structure to 32-bit socket numbers were set aside until the NCP could be overhauled.

tldr.problem: The NCP protocol only says the low-order bit of a socket number marks gender (send or receive). Two proposals wanted more network-wide structure: a user number for accounting and access control, and zero high-order 16 bits to help small hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The authors argue that socket numbers should be unique and repeatable, that each host can manage this internally by dividing its own socket space, and that a uniform network-wide split of the 32 bits is not practical.
tldr.outcome: They recommend setting both proposals aside until serious consideration can be given to a major NCP Protocol overhaul.

facts.value: Low-order bit of the socket number

sections.title: Two Proposals and a Recommendation
sections.content:
The current NCP Protocol says nothing about how hosts should assign socket numbers to process ports, except that the low-order bit specifies socket gender (send or receive). Two recent proposals called for further network-wide conventions on the 32-bit socket number.

The first asked that part of the socket number be reserved for a network-unique user number, for accounting and access control. The second asked that the high-order 16 bits be zero, to help smaller hosts reduce the space needed for socket number tables.

The RFC recommends setting both aside. Adequate handles for accounting and access control would need a large perturbation of the NCP Protocol, and the socket number is already underpowered for its use.
sections.eli5: Two people wanted to add new rules to mailbox numbers. The authors say it is better to wait and redo the whole system.

sections.title: Unique and Repeatable Sockets
sections.content:
Socket numbers identify process ports when connections are made. They must be unique to avoid ambiguity, and their assignment to specific processes should be repeatable so a process can reconnect regularly. The simplest access control is an NCP that checks its table of active connections for duplicates when a process asks for a specific socket number.

Repeatability is harder. Some sockets are universally known and tied to protocols, such as a logger socket, an RJB socket or a file transfer socket. Others are handed out during the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) exchange over the logger socket. Concurrent copies of a program need distinct identifiers, so sockets generally have to be allocated dynamically by the system.
sections.eli5: Each mailbox number must belong to only one house, and a family should get the same number each time. Some numbers are famous, like the fire station, and others are told to you when you ask.

sections.title: Partitioning the Socket Space
sections.content:
Keeping a list of every assigned socket is called a bad way, like keeping track of magnetic tape reels. With plenty of socket numbers, sparse assignment lets simple algorithms decide whether a requested socket can be allocated, looking at whether it is in a live connection, whether it is reserved as a standard service port, and how its access attributes compare with the requester's.

One good strategy is to partition a host's socket space among its users, optionally with a utility partition for sockets where repeatability is not essential. The RFC suggests viewing a socket number as three fields: a user field for repeatability, a process field for uniqueness among concurrent instances, and a tag field for multiple connections of one process.

Such fields need not be uniform across the network. The 32-bit socket number is always handled with the 8-bit host number, so if each host keeps its own sockets unique and repeatable, the whole network does too. A host that fails only affects connections with itself.
sections.eli5: Each town can split up its own mailbox numbers however it likes, as long as it does not give out the same number twice.

sections.title: Is Uniqueness Needed at All?
sections.content:
The RFC notes a suggestion that socket uniqueness may not be needed, since the socket number is hardly used once a connection is open. A host only has to save it for the life of the connection to include it in the CLOSE.

If that is true, the NCP Protocol could gain a new CLOSE that uses the host-line pair of the connection. Hosts short on space could then forget a socket number right after a successful connection. The discussion also expects that a more powerful identification mechanism, such as hierarchical names of arbitrary length, will eventually be needed.
sections.eli5: If you only need the mailbox number to say goodbye, maybe a different goodbye would let small computers forget the number sooner.
